subject: Critical Thinking
title: Rosalind Franklin: Evidence Stolen, Credit Denied
description: Learn Rosalind Franklin: Evidence Stolen, Credit Denied in one minute.

hook.text: Watson and Crick became famous, but Franklin's X-ray images made DNA's structure visible.

buildup.text: Franklin's Photo 51 – the clearest X-ray image of DNA – was the critical evidence for the double helix.

discovery.text: Maurice Wilkins showed Photo 51 to Watson without Franklin's permission.

twist.text: Franklin died at 37 from cancer. Watson and Crick won the Nobel in 1962. The rules didn't allow posthumous awards.

climax.text: Her lesson: evidence is the real hero of science.

punchline.text: She produced the evidence that solved DNA. History credited the men who used it.

quiz.question: Why is Rosalind Franklin significant in the DNA discovery?
options: She built the first DNA model
Her X-ray crystallography data (Photo 51) was the critical evidence for the double helix structure

details.summary: Rosalind Franklin's X-ray crystallography provided the crucial evidence for DNA's double helix structure. Watson and Crick used her data without her knowledge or credit, making her story a case study in how bias distorts the recognition of evidence.
details.whyItMatters: Franklin's story reveals how social biases can suppress evidence and deny credit, reminding us that critical thinking must also address the social structures of knowledge production.
takeaways: Franklin's Photo 51 was essential evidence for the DNA structure
Her contribution was used without proper acknowledgment
Bias in science can distort who gets credit for discoveries

faq.question: How important was Rosalind Franklin's evidence to the discovery of DNA's structure?
faq.answer: Franklin's Photo 51, an X-ray diffraction image, provided the key evidence. Watson later admitted that seeing this photograph was the critical moment. Without her data, the double helix model would not have been proposed when it was.

faq.question: Why was Rosalind Franklin not awarded the Nobel Prize for her contribution?
faq.answer: Franklin died of ovarian cancer in 1958, four years before the 1962 Nobel Prize. Nobel Prizes are not awarded posthumously, and during her lifetime, her contribution was systematically minimized by the male-dominated scientific establishment.
